first.rationale: The two observed declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are the mechanism most directly tied to the primary objective, and two inherited memories (86, 31) point at that lever, so it is the best-supported single-slot bet. I am spending the verification budget on those two rather than on the competitor-response option because they are the memories I would actually be acting on, and because they are the ones whose consolidated form has lost the most detail: both are outcome summaries with no effect size, no time horizon, and no statement of whether the lift persisted past week one or converted into paid, qualified revenue. Memory_31 in particular describes 'cutting required fields at signup,' which is exactly the kind of change that can improve a proximate metric while degrading something downstream — fewer qualification fields means weaker routing, and memory_44 says the sales-assisted enterprise path is where pipeline quality actually comes from. So a signup-field reduction could lift activation counts while quietly shrinking qualified enterprise pipeline; that is the specific risk the archive pull needs to resolve. I am deliberately not defaulting to promotional_pricing despite the competitor pressure: memory_73 reports acquisition and revenue lift but says nothing about margin, retention, or whether the acquired accounts were qualified, and discount-led acquisition is the classic case of a short-horizon win that erodes sustainable revenue. If verification shows memory_86's gain was measured only on completion rate rather than on downstream conversion, or that memory_31's 'durable lift' was never tracked past first week, I will narrow to a guarded test and instrument paid conversion and enterprise routing as primary metrics rather than treating onboarding completion as the win condition. I am treating all six memories as summaries whose original caveats have been stripped, not as settled facts.

final.rationale: Verification largely supported the intended direction but sharpened which version of it to run. exp_86 (shortening the onboarding flow) is the cleanest record available: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3% — a proximate metric gain that moved a durable metric in the same direction rather than trading against it. That is the profile I want when the objective is sustainable qualified revenue, and it maps directly onto the observed -4% onboarding completion and -6% activation. exp_31 came back more qualified than its consolidated summary implied: the lift is real (activation +9%, qualified revenue +4%) but retention was -1%, and the record explicitly says it holds on SMB and was not replicated on other segments. The consolidated memory had dropped both the retention cost and the scope limit. So I am running the flow-shortening intervention from exp_86, not the signup-field-cutting intervention from exp_31. This matters for the downstream risk I flagged earlier: cutting required signup fields is what would degrade qualification data and threaten the sales-assisted enterprise path that memory_44 credits with pipeline quality. Shortening the post-signup flow does not touch that routing information, so I keep the activation gain without eroding the enterprise motion. Guardrails: hold the enterprise demo-request path and its qualification fields unchanged; segment results SMB vs. non-SMB rather than reading a blended number, since exp_31 shows this company's onboarding effects do not generalize across segments; and treat paid conversion and 30-day retention as the read-out, with completion rate as a diagnostic only. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: exp_86 never reported qualified revenue directly, so its retention gain is a proxy, and both records are old enough (day 52, day 12) that the competitor's entry pricing was not in the environment when they ran — a completion gain may convert less well now that price-sensitive SMBs have an alternative. I declined promotional_pricing not because it is wrong but because memory_73 remains unverified and reports acquisition and revenue lift with no margin or retention data; discount-led acquisition is precisely where a short-horizon win can consume long-term qualified revenue, and I had no budget left to check it. If the onboarding test underperforms on paid conversion despite lifting completion, the competitor-response question should be reopened with memory_73's source pulled first.
